# Motivation {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## Education is a service market {.smaller}

- Education is one of the **world's largest service markets**, roughly **4-5% of global GDP**, about **USD 4.4-5.6 trillion a year**, serving **billions of student "consumers"** (UNESCO 2024)
- Within this market, participation in science is **skewed by gender**

::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

### The gap

- Women are only **35%** of STEM graduates worldwide
- In **India** (our setting), women are **43%** of undergraduates, **29%** of STEM students, and fewer than **18%** of the scientific workforce

:::::

::::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

### The belief

- "**Science is for boys**" takes hold **by age six** (Bian, Leslie & Cimpian 2017)
- Beliefs about **who belongs** gate entry and persistence **upstream**, beyond test scores (Cheryan et al. 2017)

:::::
:::::::::

::: {.callout-important .fragment icon="false"}
If stereotypes gate participation upstream, moving **beliefs** can matter as much as moving **scores**.
:::

## Three families of prior interventions {.smaller}

::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="33%" .fragment}

### 1. Push campaigns

- Awareness and mass messaging
- Public service announcements

**Goal:** persuade people to reconsider stereotypes

<div style="font-size: 0.62em; color:#888; margin-top: 8px;">e.g., Paluck et al. 2021; Mukhopadhyay et al. 2024</div>

:::::

::::: {.column width="33%" .fragment}

### 2. Girls-only programs

- After-school STEM, mentoring
- Separation as confidence-building

**Goal:** close information gaps, build exposure

<div style="font-size: 0.62em; color:#888; margin-top: 8px;">e.g., Dubetz & Wilson 2013; Scott & White 2013</div>

:::::

::::: {.column width="33%" .fragment}

### 3. Gender-congruent cues

- Female role models
- Identity-affirming classrooms

**Goal:** counter the masculine coding of science

<div style="font-size: 0.62em; color:#888; margin-top: 8px;">e.g., Breda et al. 2023; Master et al. 2016</div>

:::::
:::::::::

::: {.callout-warning .fragment}
## The common blind spot
All three **position gender as the problem** and work through persuasion or identity cues, which can trigger **reactance** and heighten gender salience. And they **rarely engage boys**, the classmates and teammates whose beliefs shape whether girls feel they belong (Leaper & Brown 2008).
:::

## Our reframing: redesign the service, not the message {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 4px; margin-bottom: 10px;"}
We treat STEM enrichment as an **educational service** and change **two dimensions of how it is delivered**.
:::

::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

### How students participate

**Experiential, hands-on** science, in place of chalk-and-talk instruction

:::::

::::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

### With whom they participate

**Mixed-gender** teams, in place of gender-segregated classrooms

:::::
:::::::::

::: {.callout-note .fragment icon="false"}
## Today's question
Can redesigning these two dimensions reduce gender stereotypes as a **collateral benefit**, with a **gender-neutral** program that never makes gender the stated focus?
:::

## Research questions {#research-questions .smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 1.02em; margin-top: 4px; margin-bottom: 10px;"}
We ask four questions about redesigning the **science learning experience** itself, each one answered by a different study.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-bottom: 24px;"}
**RQ1. Effect.** Does experiential, mixed-gender science instruction reduce gender-stereotype attitudes, and raise science knowledge, without ever making gender the stated focus?
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-bottom: 24px;"}
**RQ2. Heterogeneity.** Is there heterogeneity in the effect of stereotype reduction, for instance across student gender?
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-bottom: 24px;"}
**RQ3. Design.** Which features carry the effect, experiential pedagogy, mixed-gender grouping, or the two together?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**RQ4. Mechanism.** Through what psychological process does contact move beliefs, the affective route (empathy, reduced anxiety) or the cognitive route (trust, knowledge)?
:::

## Roadmap: a multi-method approach {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="33%"}

### Study 1
**Field intervention**

<div style="color:#990000; font-weight:700; font-size:0.9em; margin:2px 0 6px;">Answers RQ1 &amp; RQ2</div>

- 156 schools, Grade 6
- Difference-in-differences
- Does it work, and for whom?

:::::

::::: {.column width="33%" .fragment}

### Study 2
**2 x 2 experiment**

<div style="color:#990000; font-weight:700; font-size:0.9em; margin:2px 0 6px;">Answers RQ3</div>

- N = 1,207
- Which features do the work?

:::::

::::: {.column width="33%" .fragment}

### Study 3
**Mechanism experiment**

<div style="color:#990000; font-weight:700; font-size:0.9em; margin:2px 0 6px;">Answers RQ4</div>

- N = 605
- Why does it work?

:::::
::::::::::

# Conceptual Framework {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## A services lens on educational impact {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

The social impact of a service depends not only on **what it delivers** but on **how it is structured**.

- Prior service research: delivery shapes the customer experience and intended outcomes (Bitner 1992; Lemon & Verhoef 2016)
- Our claim: delivery can also shape **how consumers perceive the people they interact with**

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
Science learning is the focal outcome; **belief change about who belongs** emerges alongside it, as a collateral social consequence of the service structure.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Two dimensions of service delivery {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

### How consumers participate

Customer-participation research: how consumers engage in production and delivery (Yim et al. 2012).

In our setting: **experiential, hands-on** learning.

:::::

::::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

### With whom they participate

Shared-consumption research: how other consumers shape the experience (Bhargave & Montgomery 2013).

In our setting: **mixed-gender** grouping.

:::::
::::::::::

::: {.callout-important .fragment}
We study these **jointly**. The question is whether their effects are interdependent, not simply additive.
:::

## Intergroup contact theory {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="52%"}

Allport's (1954) conditions for **prejudice-reducing** contact:

1. Equal group status within the situation
2. Common goals
3. Intergroup cooperation
4. Support of authority

Pettigrew & Tropp (2006, 2008): contact works, and **affect** carries more of the effect than cognition.

:::::

::::: {.column width="48%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## The key insight
Experiential science in mixed-gender teams supplies **all four conditions** as a **byproduct of the pedagogy**, not as a gender program.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Experiential learning: Kolb's cycle {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}

<img src="images/experiential-learning-cycle.jpg" style="width: 100%; max-height: 560px; object-fit: contain;"/>

:::::

::::: {.column width="50%"}

- **Concrete experience:** students manipulate real equipment
- **Reflective observation:** they discuss what they saw
- **Abstract conceptualization:** they draw conclusions
- **Active experimentation:** they test and iterate

<div style="font-size: 0.8em; color:#555;">Distinct from acquiring and recalling abstract symbols (Kolb 1984).</div>

:::::
::::::::::

## Conceptual model {.smaller}

<div style="text-align:center;">
<img src="images/conceptual_model_flowchart.png" style="width: 82%; max-height: 640px; object-fit: contain;"/>
</div>

# Study 1: Field Intervention {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## Our Study Context {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
- Public schools serve **over 70%** of India's students, and **more than half** of Grade 9-10 students attend schools **without proper science labs**
:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
- Instruction is **chalk-and-talk**, only **14%** of classrooms use materials beyond the textbook, and students sit in **gender-segregated rows**
:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
- Our setting is **Bodoland, Assam**, spanning all five districts (Kokrajhar, Chirang, Baksa, Tamulpur, Udalguri)
:::

:::::

::::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2"}

</div>

## The intervention: Mobile Science Labs {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="48%"}

### What the program adds

- A non-profit brings a **Mobile Science Lab**, a van with lab equipment and two instructors, to rural government schools
- **Ten 2-hour hands-on sessions** plus two assessments over the year, about **20 added hours** of science
- Curriculum spans Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and Math, built on **Kolb's experiential cycle**
- Students work in **mixed-gender groups** on equipment they otherwise never access

<div style="font-size: 0.74em; color:#888; margin-top:12px;">The program never mentions gender. It is a science program.</div>

:::::

::::: {.column width="52%"}

## A mobile science lab close to home {#bloomington-msl .smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="1"}
<img src="images/bloomington_stem_lab.jpg" style="width: 100%; max-height: 380px; object-fit: cover; border-radius: 6px; box-shadow: 0 3px 10px rgba(0,0,0,0.22);"/>

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1"}
<img src="images/nebraska_mobile_lab.jpg" style="width: 100%; max-height: 380px; object-fit: cover; border-radius: 6px; box-shadow: 0 3px 10px rgba(0,0,0,0.22);"/>

<div style="font-size: 0.62em; color:#888; text-align:center; margin-top: 4px;">Husker Mobile Beef & Science Lab, University of Nebraska-Lincoln</div>

:::::

::::: {.column width="44%"}

### The same delivery model

::: {.r-stack style="align-items: start; justify-items: start;"}

::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="1" style="text-align: left;"}
In **Indiana**, Monroe County schools run a *STEM to Them Mobile Lab*, a vehicle that brings hands-on science into classrooms.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1" style="text-align: left;"}
In **Nebraska**, this university runs the *Mobile Beef & Science Lab* out of its Ithaca center (ENREEC), taking a science classroom and agricultural science on the road.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
The format we study is **not unique to rural India**. A version runs in my backyard, and one runs right here, out of **Nebraska**.
:::
:::

:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Data and sample {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="52%"}

### Grade 6 sample

- **N = 2,779 students**, **156 schools** in Bodoland
- Treatment: **2,171** students, **108** schools
- Control: **608** students, **48** matched schools
- **Two-wave panel:** baseline and endline within the year

:::::

::::: {.column width="48%" .fragment}

### Two primary outcomes

- **Gender-stereotype attitude:** "Science is for boys more than girls," 1-5
- **Science knowledge:** percent of grade-aligned items correct, 0-100

<div style="font-size:0.78em; color:#555; margin-top:8px;">Plus a broader battery of science-attitude measures, covering interest, self-efficacy, and intentions to pursue a science career.</div>

:::::
::::::::::

## We also have Grades 7-8 for treated schools, but focus on Grade 6 {.smaller}

- The partner surveyed treated students in **Grades 6, 7, and 8**, but control schools **only at Grade 6**
- Grade 6 is the **sole cohort** with both treated and control students, so it is the clean **common-support** sample
- Restricting to one cohort also holds **age constant** across arms

::: {.fragment}
Results for the **pooled sample that also includes Grades 7 and 8 remain consistent**.
:::

# Identification & Robustness {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## The core threat: non-random selection {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

- Treatment schools were chosen by the implementing partner from a government list, on **school strength, distance from the vehicle route, and language of instruction**
- Control schools were **not randomly assigned**
- So treated and control schools may differ on dimensions that affect learning and attitudes

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-warning icon="false"}
Our strategy: make the arms comparable on observables (matching, reweighting), bound the role of unobservables (Oster), and stress-test inference.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Building the control group {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

**Coarsened exact matching** on twelve school characteristics observed before the program:

- Ten matched **exactly**, including **pincode** (geography)
- Two on **coarsened bins** (reading-corner books, total teachers)
- 92% of control schools share a pincode with a treated school

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
Matching addresses **observed** school differences. Student fixed effects and reweighting handle the rest.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Pre-treatment balance {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.58em; width: 92%; margin: 0 auto;"}
**School characteristics** (the variables we matched on)

| Variable | Matched | Treatment | Control | SMD | $p$ |
|------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Kuchcha building present | Exact | 0.16 | 0.06 | 0.31 | .123 |
| Co-educational | Exact | 0.95 | 1.00 | $-$0.31 | .324 |
| School toilet present | Exact | 0.97 | 1.00 | $-$0.24 | .553 |
| Playground facility | Exact | 0.91 | 0.98 | $-$0.31 | .174 |
| Dilapidated classroom present | Exact | 0.21 | 0.35 | $-$0.31 | .076 |
| Reading-corner books | Coarse | 58.33 | 30.92 | 0.15 | .313 |
| Total teachers (size proxy) | Coarse | 14.26 | 10.12 | 0.47 | .003 |
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.58em; width: 92%; margin: 12px auto 0;"}
**Student outcomes** (not used in matching)

| Outcome (pre-treatment) | Treatment | Control | SMD | $p$ |
|------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Gender-stereotype attitude | 2.98 | 2.84 | 0.10 | .026 |
| Science knowledge, 0-100 | 19.14 | 26.27 | $-$0.36 | $<.001$ |
:::

<div style="font-size: 0.66em; color:#555; text-align:center; margin-top:10px;">Matching balances schools on their observed characteristics, but the student outcomes, which we never matched on, still differ. Identification therefore rests on within-student change and reweighting, not on the raw cross-section.</div>

## Model-free evidence {.smaller}

<div style="text-align:center;">
<img src="images/model_free_grade6.png" style="width: 74%; max-height: 640px; object-fit: contain;"/>
</div>

<div style="font-size: 0.78em; color:#555; text-align:center;">Stereotype: treated 2.98 to 2.08, control 2.84 to 2.76. Knowledge: treated 19 to 39, control stays near 25.</div>

## Estimation {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="52%"}

Difference-in-differences with **student and period fixed effects**:

$$Y_{it} = \beta\,(Trt_s \times Post_t) + \alpha_i + \tau_t + \varepsilon_{it}$$

- $\beta$ (Treatment $\times$ Post) is the **causal effect**
- **Student** FE $\alpha_i$: within-student change
- **Period** FE $\tau_t$
- **SEs clustered at the school level** (assignment level)

:::::

::::: {.column width="48%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
Identification comes from **within-student change** over the two waves, differenced against the matched control group.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Main results: difference-in-differences {.smaller}

:::: columns

::: {.column width="72%"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.72em;"}
<p style="text-align: center; font-weight: bold; color: #990000;">Panel A: Gender-Stereotype Attitude (1-5)</p>

|  | No FE | School FE | Student + Period FE |
|------|------|------|------|
| [**Treatment × Post**]{.my-crimson} | -0.816<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | -0.785<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | **-0.786<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup>** |
|  | (0.200) | (0.202) | (0.203) |
| N (student-waves) | 5,407 | 5,407 | 5,258 |
| R² | .093 | .275 | .568 |

<p style="text-align: center; font-weight: bold; color: #990000;">Panel B: Science Knowledge Score (0-100)</p>

|  | No FE | School FE | Student + Period FE |
|------|------|------|------|
| [**Treatment × Post**]{.my-crimson} | 20.58<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | 20.58<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | **20.58<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup>** |
|  | (3.13) | (3.13) | (3.13) |
| N (student-waves) | 5,558 | 5,558 | 5,558 |

<p style="text-align: center;">*SEs clustered at the school level; <sup>&ast;</sup>p<.05, <sup>&ast;&ast;</sup>p<.01, <sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup>p<.001. Column (3) is primary.*</p>
:::
:::

::: {.column width="28%"}

::: {.callout-important .fragment}
## Stereotypes
**-0.79 points**

≈ **0.61 SD**, a **quarter** of the control baseline; stable across specifications
:::

::: {.callout-tip .fragment}
## Knowledge
**+20.6 points**

large and significant; treated students overtake control by endline
:::

:::

::::

## Robustness I: reweighting {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em; width: 72%; margin: 0 auto;"}
| Specification | Estimate | 95% CI |
|------|------|------|
| Student + period FE (primary) | -0.786<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | [-1.18, -0.39] |
| School fixed effects | -0.785<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | [-1.18, -0.39] |
| Inverse-propensity weighting | -0.875<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | [-1.32, -0.43] |
| Entropy balancing | -0.824<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | [-1.27, -0.38] |
| Doubly-robust DiD (AIPW) | -0.827<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> | [-1.18, -0.48] |
:::

<div style="font-size: 0.78em; color:#555; text-align:center; margin-top:8px;">Reweighting on six baseline covariates leaves the effect **at least as large**. The doubly-robust estimator is consistent if either the propensity or outcome model is correct.</div>

## Robustness II: selection on unobservables {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="52%"}

**Oster (2019)** coefficient-stability logic:

- Short regression (no FE): $\beta = -0.816$, $R^2 = .093$
- Long regression (school FE): $\beta = -0.785$, $R^2 = .275$
- Under $R_{\max} = 1.3 \times R^2_{\text{long}}$, the bias-adjusted effect is $-0.771$

:::::

::::: {.column width="48%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## How much selection would it take?
Unobservables would need to be about **56 times** as strong as all observed covariates combined to explain the effect away.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Robustness III: small-sample inference {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

With relatively **few control clusters**, conventional clustered SEs could overstate significance. We confirm with:

- School-level **permutation test**: $p = .004$
- **CR2** (Satterthwaite) correction: $p < .001$
- Restricted **wild cluster bootstrap**: $p = .002$

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
Design-based and small-sample inference all reject the null. The result does not hinge on the clustered-SE asymptotics.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## The parallel-trends question {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

With a **single pre-period**, parallel trends **cannot be tested**. We say so plainly. Two pieces of evidence bear on it:

- The **control group barely moves** over the year (2.84 to 2.76), an order of magnitude below the treatment effect
- The effect does **not concentrate** among high-baseline students (no regression-to-the-mean signature)

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-warning icon="false"}
Neither fact tests parallel trends. Together they make **natural drift** an unlikely explanation for an effect of this size.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Robustness IV: linguistic composition {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

A concern: treated and control schools might differ in **language and culture** (Bodoland is linguistically mixed).

- Medium of instruction was a **matching variable**; both arms are **96-98% Assamese- or Bodo-medium**
- Restricting to those schools gives an estimate of **-0.69** (S.E. 0.20), essentially unchanged

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
The effect is **not an artifact of linguistic composition** across arms.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

# Heterogeneity & Additional Outcomes {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## Heterogeneity by student gender {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="52%"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.78em;"}
|  | Gender-Stereotype | Science Knowledge |
|------|:------:|:------:|
| [**Treat × Post × Male**]{.my-crimson} | **-0.556<sup>&ast;</sup>** | -0.725 |
|  | p = .012 | p = .833 |
| Treat × Post | -0.550<sup>&ast;</sup> | 20.952<sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup> |
| Post × Male | 0.540<sup>&ast;&ast;</sup> | -1.275 |

<div style="font-size:0.9em;">*Student + period FE; <sup>&ast;</sup>p<.05, <sup>&ast;&ast;</sup>p<.01, <sup>&ast;&ast;&ast;</sup>p<.001.*</div>
:::

:::::

::::: {.column width="48%" .fragment}

- **Stereotype reduction ~2x larger for boys**
- **Knowledge gains equal** across gender
- Consistent with contact theory: those who **hold** the stereotype update most

:::::
::::::::::

## Marginal effects by gender {.smaller}

<div style="text-align:center;">
<img src="images/marginal_did_gender_grade6.png" style="width: 72%; max-height: 600px; object-fit: contain;"/>
</div>

<div style="font-size: 0.78em; color:#555; text-align:center;">Stereotype: boys -1.11 [-1.55, -0.66], girls -0.55 [-1.00, -0.10]. Knowledge: statistically equal.</div>

## Not a floor effect {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

A natural worry: boys move more only because they start higher.

- Boys and girls begin at **nearly identical baselines**: **2.96** vs **2.94**, both near the scale midpoint
- Floor shares are similar: **17%** of boys, **14%** of girls at the floor

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
Boys do not simply have more room to move. The asymmetry reflects **contact theory's out-group logic**: boys hold the stereotype about girls in science.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Heterogeneity by school context {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
<img src="images/marginal_DiD_vs_SchoolSize_gs.png" style="width: 100%; max-height: 400px; object-fit: contain;"/>
<div style="font-size:0.72em; color:#555; text-align:center;">Larger stereotype reductions in bigger schools (p = .027).</div>
:::
::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
<img src="images/marginal_DiD_vs_GirlsShare_gs.png" style="width: 100%; max-height: 400px; object-fit: contain;"/>
<div style="font-size:0.72em; color:#555; text-align:center;">No moderation by the girls' share of the grade.</div>
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note .fragment icon="false"}
The effect does not depend on a particular gender ratio, but it is somewhat stronger where more students are exposed together.
:::

## Effects extend beyond the two outcomes {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="58%"}

### Broader science attitudes (14 items)

<img src="images/forest_grade6.png" style="width: 100%; max-height: 600px; object-fit: contain;"/>

<div style="font-size: 0.72em; color:#555; text-align:center;">All 14 items move positively and are individually significant.</div>

:::::

::::: {.column width="42%" .fragment}

### Perceptions of excellence

A projective vignette: is a described top student a boy or a girl?

- Science: **β = 0.55** (p < .001)
- Language arts: **β = 0.45** (p < .001), a placebo domain

The shift reaches **who belongs**, and extends **beyond science**.

:::::
::::::::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<div style="text-align:center; font-weight:bold; color:#990000;">High-performing science student</div>

# Study 2: Isolating the Mechanism {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## Why we need experiments {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

The field program **bundles** several features at once:

- Experiential, hands-on pedagogy
- **Mixed-gender** collaborative grouping
- Equal-status peer interaction
- Extended exposure

The field data **cannot isolate** which feature drives the effect, nor the psychological process.

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Two pre-registered experiments
**Study 2** separates the design features.<br>
**Study 3** traces the mechanism.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Study 2: design {#study2 .smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="48%"}

### A 2 x 2 between-subjects design

- **N = 1,207** US adults (CloudResearch), pre-registered
- **Gender grouping:** single vs. mixed
- **Instruction:** standard vs. experiential
- Participants imagine being a student in a described school

:::::

::::: {.column width="52%" .fragment}

### The measure

Projective **gender-stereotypical behavioral preference** (Good 2001), 1-7:

> "To what extent would the average student prefer to have **men** on their team, not women?"

Asking about the **average student** reduces socially desirable responding.

:::::
::::::::::

<div style="font-size:0.6em; text-align:right; color:#777;">[Study 2 details &amp; full stats](#study2-details)</div>

## Study 2: main effects {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

Both features help **on their own**:

- **Grouping:** mixed **3.83** vs single **4.17**, $F(1,1203) = 19.34$, $p < .001$
- **Instruction:** experiential **3.87** vs standard **4.13**, $F(1,1203) = 10.82$, $p = .001$

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
Main effects are real but modest. The question is whether the two features are **complementary**.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Study 2: the interaction {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.r-stack}

<img src="images/study2_interaction.png" style="width: 94%;"/>

<img src="images/study2_grouping.png" class="fragment" style="width: 94%;"/>

:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

::: {.callout-tip}
## The interaction (p = .048)
Mixed-gender grouping cuts stereotypes **mainly under experiential** instruction (3.62 vs. 4.12), about **two and a half times** the gap under standard instruction.
:::

<div style="font-size: 0.78em; color:#555;">$F(1,1203) = 3.91$, $p = .048$. Equivalently, experiential learning helps only when groups are **mixed**.</div>

:::
::::

# Study 3: Mechanisms {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## Why Study 3 {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

Study 2 shows the two features work **together**. Study 3 asks **why**.

- Contact theory names four processes: two **affective**, two **cognitive**
- We test which ones **carry** the effect
- Design **mirrors the field contrast**: standard, gender-segregated vs. mixed-gender experiential

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Design
**N = 605** US adults, pre-registered, two conditions.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

<div style="font-size:0.6em; text-align:right; color:#777;">[Study 3 details &amp; measures](#study3-details)</div>

## Study 3: the four contact mechanisms {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}

### Affective

- [**Empathy**]{style="color:#1B7F4B;"} toward the other gender (Swart et al. 2011)
- [**Reduced anxiety**]{style="color:#1B7F4B;"} about cross-gender interaction (Wolfer et al. 2019)

:::::

::::: {.column width="50%"}

### Cognitive

- [**Trust**]{style="color:#2C6FB5;"} of the other gender (Turner et al. 2007)
- [**Knowledge**]{style="color:#2C6FB5;"} about the other gender (Zagefka et al. 2017)

:::::
::::::::::

::: {.callout-note .fragment}
All four are measured with **established multi-item scales** ($\alpha$ from .88 to .94), in a projective frame.
:::

## Study 3: condition means {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
<img src="images/study3_means.png" style="width: 100%; max-height: 600px; object-fit: contain;"/>
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}

Mixed-gender experiential learning:

- Replicates the field effect: stereotypes **4.13 to 3.37**
- Moves **all four** mechanisms in the predicted direction (all $p < .001$)

::: {.callout-note .fragment}
Each mechanism also **mediates** the effect when tested on its own.
:::

:::
::::

## Study 3: what carries the effect {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="64%"}

<img src="images/mediation_diagram_colored.png" style="width: 100%; max-height: 600px; object-fit: contain;"/>

:::::

::::: {.column width="36%"}

With all four entered **together**, only the **affective** routes survive:

- [**Empathy**]{style="color:#1B7F4B;"}: indirect **-.083** [-.159, -.026]
- [**Reduced anxiety**]{style="color:#1B7F4B;"}: **-.122** [-.202, -.054]
- [**Trust**]{style="color:#2C6FB5;"} and [**knowledge**]{style="color:#2C6FB5;"} attenuate to non-significance

:::::
::::::::::

## Interpretation: affect over cognition {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

- The effect runs through **greater empathy** and **reduced anxiety** toward the other gender
- Trust and knowledge move, but do not **carry** the effect once affect is in the model
- Consistent with **Pettigrew & Tropp (2008)**: affect mediates contact effects more than cognition

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
Working shoulder to shoulder changes **how students feel** about one another before it changes **what they know**.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

# Discussion {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## Summary of findings {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 6px;"}
The social impact of an educational service depends on both **what is delivered** and **how it is structured**.
:::

- **Study 1:** experiential, mixed-gender delivery **improves learning** while reducing gender stereotypes as a **collateral outcome**, by about a quarter (-0.79, -0.61 SD), twice as much for boys
- **Study 2:** the two features are **complementary**, not independently sufficient
- **Study 3:** the effect operates through **intergroup empathy and reduced anxiety**

## Theoretical implications {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

### Service design shapes beliefs

Service delivery can shape **how consumers perceive one another**, beyond the focal outcome. Two dimensions, how and with whom, act **jointly**.

:::::

::::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

### Learn with and about others

Shared experiences let consumers **learn not only with others, but about others**, updating beliefs about co-consumers and the groups they represent.

:::::
::::::::::

## Contribution to gender and STEM education {.smaller}

:::::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="55%"}

- Prior interventions target **girls' interest, confidence, or participation** directly
- We show gender beliefs can shift in **gender-neutral** environments when delivery creates **cross-gender collaboration**
- The approach **reaches boys**, whom girls-only formats leave untouched

:::::

::::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
The **social organization of learning** deserves attention alongside curriculum content and instructional quality.
:::

:::::
::::::::::

## Implications for policy and practice {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="62%"}

- India's **National Education Policy** emphasizes experiential learning as a pedagogy; our results give a **second rationale**, belief change
- Treat **mixed-gender grouping** as a design principle, and evaluate programs on **belief change alongside test scores**
- For funders: a way to shift beliefs among **boys and girls**, not just self-selected participants

:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
<div style="text-align:center;">
<img src="images/SDG.png" style="width: 90%; max-height: 420px; object-fit: contain;"/>
</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.72em; color:#555; text-align:center;">A scalable lever for SDG 4 and 5.</div>
:::
::::

## Limitations {.smaller}

1. **Self-reported beliefs**, not downstream enrollment or careers; longitudinal follow-up is needed
2. The field intervention **bundles** features (Study 2 separates them in the lab; a field factorial would be stronger)
3. **Rural public-school** setting; generalizability to urban and private settings is open
4. The field stereotype measure is a **single item**; Studies 2 and 3 use different, multi-item operationalizations

## Thank you {.center data-background-color="#FFFFFF"}

# Appendix {visibility="uncounted" background-color="#FFFFFF"}

## Study 1: primary outcome measures {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Gender-stereotype attitude

> **"I feel science is for boys more than girls."**

- 5-point Likert (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)
- Higher = stronger endorsement
- A single, concrete, direct belief

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Science knowledge score

- Standardized, grade-appropriate assessment
- Chemistry, physics, biology aligned to the state curriculum
- Scored as percent correct (0-100), authored by the program provider

:::
:::

## Study 1: robustness of the knowledge effect {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

The raw **+20.6** point gain attenuates under matching and reweighting on baseline proficiency, but stays large and significant.

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em; width: 70%; margin: 0 auto;"}
| Specification | Estimate | 95% CI |
|------|------|------|
| Student + period FE (primary) | 20.58 | [14.46, 26.71] |
| School fixed effects | 20.58 | [14.46, 26.71] |
| Inverse-propensity weighting | 14.53 | [7.95, 21.10] |
| Entropy balancing | 15.83 | [9.27, 22.39] |
| Doubly-robust DiD (AIPW) | 15.52 | [7.47, 23.58] |
:::

<div style="font-size: 0.74em; color:#555; text-align:center;">The stereotype effect was never confounded by the pre-period knowledge gap.</div>

## Study 1: response-category decomposition {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

The treatment shifts the **whole distribution** toward disagreement:

- Probability of the lowest category (strongly disagree) rises by **.234** (p < .001)
- Probability of disagreeing overall (1 or 2) rises by **.31** (p < .001)
- Probability of agreeing overall (4 or 5) falls by **.18** (p = .004)
- An ordered probit implies the same monotone shift

## Study 1: pooled Grade 6-8 (for transparency) {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em; width: 72%; margin: 0 auto;"}
| Specification | Estimate | S.E. |
|------|:------:|:------:|
| No fixed effects | -0.595 | 0.186 |
| School fixed effects | -0.576 | 0.188 |
| School-by-grade fixed effects | -0.573 | 0.188 |
| Student + period fixed effects | -0.571 | 0.188 |
:::

<div style="font-size: 0.74em; color:#555; text-align:center;">Pooled N = 10,214. Smaller than the Grade 6 estimate and identified partly from cross-grade comparisons that lack common support, which is why the main text restricts to Grade 6.</div>

## Study 1: predictors of baseline endorsement {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em; width: 74%; margin: 0 auto;"}
| Predictor | Estimate | S.E. | $p$ |
|------|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| Male | 0.006 | 0.064 | .919 |
| Baseline science knowledge | 0.001 | 0.002 | .495 |
| Log school size | 0.090 | 0.045 | .050 |
| Girls' share of grade | -0.150 | 0.257 | .560 |
| Teacher-student ratio | -0.336 | 0.916 | .715 |
:::

<div style="font-size: 0.74em; color:#555; text-align:center;">Baseline endorsement is not systematically predicted by student or school characteristics (joint F(5,153) = 1.99, p = .084; adjusted R² = .005).</div>

## Study 2: procedure and measure (detail) {#study2-details .smaller visibility="uncounted"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}

### Procedure

- **N = 1,207** US adults on CloudResearch Connect (M~age~ = 44, 62% female); pre-registered
- Participants **imagine being a student** in a described public school
- **Grouping:** single-gender = separate sides of the classroom; mixed-gender = sit and work together
- **Instruction:** standard = lectures and individual work; experiential = operate equipment, observe, discuss, conclude

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

### Dependent measure

> "Suppose there is a team competition to see which team is smarter in math and science. To what extent would the **average student** prefer to have men on their team, not women?"

- 1 = "not at all" to 7 = "very much so"
- Projective framing reduces socially desirable responding

:::
:::

<div style="font-size:0.6em; text-align:right; color:#777;">[Back to Study 2](#study2)</div>

## Study 2: full statistics {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

- **Main effect, grouping:** mixed 3.83 vs single 4.17, $F(1,1203) = 19.34$, $p < .001$, $\eta_p^2 = .016$
- **Main effect, instruction:** experiential 3.87 vs standard 4.13, $F(1,1203) = 10.82$, $p = .001$, $\eta_p^2 = .009$
- **Interaction:** $F(1,1203) = 3.91$, $p = .048$, $\eta_p^2 = .003$
- **Simple effect (experiential):** mixed 3.62 vs single 4.12, $p < .001$; a .50-point gap, about 2.5x the .19-point gap under standard instruction

## Study 3: procedure and measures (detail) {#study3-details .smaller visibility="uncounted"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Procedure

- **N = 605** US adults (CloudResearch; M~age~ = 43, 55% female); pre-registered
- Both conditions: school normally has "gender-segregated rows with limited cross-gender interaction"
- **Experiential condition:** a program where students of all genders work together to conduct experiments, observe, and discuss, in small mixed-gender groups

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Stereotype measure (3 items, $\alpha$ = .876)

- "Men are just better at science than women"
- "I would go to a man instead of a woman for help with a math or science problem"
- "Genders differ in their skill at science"

Projectively framed (Lane, Goh & Driver-Linn 2012).

:::
:::

<div style="font-size:0.6em; text-align:right; color:#777;">[Back to Study 3](#study3)</div>

## Study 3: condition means and mediation (detail) {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Condition means (control to experiential)

- Stereotype: 4.13 to 3.37 (p < .001)
- Trust: 3.81 to 4.45 (p < .001)
- Knowledge: 3.46 to 4.28 (p < .001)
- Empathy: 4.24 to 4.77 (p < .001)
- Anxiety: 4.68 to 4.17 (p < .001)

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Mediation (PROCESS Model 4)

**Simple (each significant):** trust -.195, knowledge -.182, empathy -.147, anxiety -.171

**Parallel (all four):**

- Empathy **-.083** [-.159, -.026]
- Anxiety **-.122** [-.202, -.054]
- Trust -.072 (n.s.), Knowledge +.030 (n.s.)

:::
:::

## Identification: summary {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

| Threat | Evidence against it |
|------|------|
| Observed school differences | CEM on 12 characteristics; balance on all |
| Baseline student differences | Within-student (student FE) design |
| Residual observed imbalance | IPW, entropy balancing, doubly-robust DiD |
| Unobserved selection | Oster bound (~56x) |
| Small-cluster inference | Permutation (.004), CR2 (<.001), wild bootstrap (.002) |
| Natural drift / pre-trends | Control-group stability; no high-baseline concentration |
| Linguistic composition | Assamese/Bodo-only estimate unchanged (-0.69) |
